content:Speaker user says: Here is a piece of text: We’ve all heard that it’s better to give than to receive. Now there’s empirical evidence to show that being compassionate to a spouse is rewarding in and of itself.
Psychologists have found that the emotional benefits of compassionate acts are significant for the giver, whether or not the recipient is even aware of the act. For example, if a husband notices that the windshield on his wife’s car is covered with snow, he may scrape it off before driving to work. That gesture would boost his emotional well-being, regardless of whether his wife notices.
Harry Reis, a professor of psychology at the University of Rochester, led a research team that studied 175 North American newlywed husbands and wives who were married an average of 7.17 months. The results have been published in the journal Emotion.
For 30 years, psychologist Harry Reis has put human relationships under the microscope.
The team of psychologists, which included Ronald Rogge of Rochester and Michael Maniaci of Florida Atlantic University, asked participants to keep a two-week daily diary to record those instances in which either spouse put aside personal wishes in order to meet the partner’s needs. But the researchers also needed to assess the emotional well-being of the individuals. To that end, the participants kept track of their daily emotional states for each day based on 14 positive and negative terms—such as enthusiastic, happy, calm, sad, angry, and hurt.
The psychologists discovered that donors benefit from compassionate acts, regardless of whether the recipient explicitly notices the acts.
Over the course of the 14 days, husbands and wives reported giving and receiving an average of .65 and .59 compassionate acts each day—with husbands perceiving more such acts than did their partners. The acts included such things as changing personal plans for the partner’s sake, doing something that showed the partner was valued, and expressing tenderness for the spouse.
Before the study, the researchers predicted that the greatest impact on the donor would come when the act was recognized by the recipient, because recognition would make the donor feel valued. They also thought the recipient would feel the most benefit when the act was mutually recognized, as opposed to those times when one partner perceived a compassionate act that wasn’t actually intended. While those predictions were confirmed, the researchers discovered something else.
The psychologists discovered that donors benefit from compassionate acts, regardless of whether the recipient explicitly notices the acts. And in those cases, the benefits for the donors was about 45 percent greater than for the recipients, as determined by the self-assessment scales in the daily diaries, with the effect being equally strong for men and women.
Reis is now working with Rochester alum Peter Caprariello, an assistant professor of marketing at Stony Brook University, to study the emotional benefits of spending money on others. Their work suggests that spending on others can make a person feel better, but only when the goal is to benefit that person. Spending to impress them with generosity or vision doesn’t do the trick.

content:Speaker user says: What are the benefits of treating your host town during a study abroad experience like home? Answer according to: Most weekends this semester, you’d find me in or around St Andrews, Scotland. Unlike many study abroad students, I have not been doing as much traveling this semester.
Don’t get me wrong: I love traveling and I think it’s a great part of your study abroad experience. Due in part to my limited finances, however, I usually spend my time much closer to school.
Last semester, I also saved most of my money from my work-study job on campus for travel and spending money. This bolstered my bank account for the inevitable costs of international travel and living in a country with a strong currency like the British pound.
Most of this money, however, I was saving for a trip in continental Europe, when I visited France, Germany, and the Netherlands by train. I had never been to these countries before and knew studying so nearby was a chance I could not pass up!
Since I am used to having a job during the school year, I looked for ways I might be able to sustaining an income while abroad. Researching my short-term student visa, I found it would not allow me to work while in the UK. Then I discovered IFSA-Butler’s work-to-study program, and I was lucky enough to get one of the positions on offer. This has helped to maintain my living money as well.
With enough financial planning and forethought, it is possible even for students heavily reliant on financial aid like myself to travel while abroad!
Despite my main trip over spring break and another weekend trip or two, however, I’m usually not far from St Andrews. And to be honest, I’m quite happy with this.
It can be hard, of course, to see other students traveling throughout the semester—that sinking feeling that perhaps you aren’t “making the most of it.” But I have grown to really appreciate what this little seaside Scottish town has to offer, and it’s begun to feel like home in just a few short months.
When I first decided to study in Scotland, it was a bit of a promised land in my mind—a new and fresh start for the semester. Then as I boarded the plane for my transatlantic flight, fears of how it couldn’t possibly live up to these high expectations flashed through my mind. Yet, since arriving here it really has. I have loved settling into my new home and treating it like just that: a new home.
Rather than using it as a base from which to explore other parts of Europe, I have enjoyed engaging more with the area itself. It’s the little things—such as a longer chat with the cashier at the grocery store about how one of her kids went to St Andrews, finding hidden park trails for relaxing walks, or having a usual order at a local pub—that really make you feel at home.
Bonding with other students usually happens rather organically, but interacting with the locals can require a bit more effort on a university student’s part. But that extra effort pays off, as you really get to know the culture of the area more, not just the university’s culture.
Plus, this part of Scotland is so beautiful that walks around town and through the countryside feel as fulfilling as a day full of traveling. Day trips hiking down the coast or visiting the various free museums and sites in nearby Edinburgh vary the routine as well, and further familiarize me with the area, all while still within my budget.
Treating my host town like home also feels like it gives me more permission to just take time off—whether it’s to read (other than for class), watch Netflix, or watch people playing on the pitches from my window. When my pace of life is already more like that of a St Andrews resident than a traveler’s, I don’t feel guilty unwinding. I don’t feel the need to always be doing something, the kind of feeling I know I often get when traveling.
Although it’s due mainly to my tight finances, sticking around St Andrews has had so many merits that I’ve come to appreciate. Most of it is from the state of mind with which I approach my situation. That is, the kind of contentment and peace you can find when you feel at home somewhere, rather than a visitor there.
This is very dependent on your preferences, of course, and what you hope to get from your study abroad experience. Still, I would highly recommend trying to strike a balance between traveling elsewhere and experiencing where you are studying, whatever your situation may be.
I know I already feel immensely attached to this place, in a way that I’m not sure I would, had I spent less time getting to know it. context:The author expresses a growing sense of contentment and belonging while studying in Scotland, particularly in the town of St Andrews. They’ve prioritized settling in and embracing the local culture, finding joy in simple activities and connecting with the community. Despite financial considerations, they’ve leveraged opportunities like a work-to-study program to maintain their income and appreciate the town’s unique atmosphere. The author’s desire for a balance between travel and local immersion highlights the importance of finding a comfortable and fulfilling experience, emphasizing that home isn’t necessarily about constant movement, but rather a state of mind and a sense of belonging. keywords: host town, study abroad, Scotland, home, financial aid, travel, student visa, St Andrews tags: host town, study abroad, Scotland, home, financial aid, travel, personal development, well-being

content:Speaker assistant says: Hello everyone! In this tutorial, I'm going to show you how to improve your balance and posture while dancing. We'll be focusing on ballet, as it's a style that put great emphasis on these qualities. Let's get started!

Step 1: Proper Body Alignment

The first thing we need to consider is body alignment. Stand with your feet hip-width apart and your shoulders relaxed. Draw your abs in and lengthen your spine, imagining your head is being lifted up by a string. Avoid arching your back or sticking your butt out. Your posture should be straight, but not rigid.

Step 2: Core Strengthening Exercises

To improve your balance, you need a strong and stable core. Here are some exercises you can do to strengthen your core:

- Planks: Start on your hands and knees, then lower yourself down into a push-up position. Your wrists, elbows, and shoulders should form a straight line. Hold for 30 seconds to 1 minute.
- Sit-ups: Lie on your back with your knees bent, feet flat on the ground, and hands behind your head. Curl your upper body towards your knees, then lower back down. Do 10-15 repetitions.
- Leg lifts: Lie on your back with your hands under your butt. Lift your legs off the floor and hold for 30 seconds. Lower your legs down, then repeat.

Step 3: Proper Footwork

Your feet are the foundation of your balance. Here are some tips to improve your footwork:

- Alignment: Make sure your feet are aligned with your knees and hips. Avoid turning your feet in or out.
- Pointe work: If you're doing ballet, make sure your toes are pointed and your weight is evenly distributed on your toes.
- Relevé: To improve your balance on relevé (standing on the balls of your feet), imagine you have a piece of paper between your big toes and keep it from falling. This will prevent you from rolling to the side.

Step 4: Putting it All Together

Now that you've mastered the basics, let's put it all together! Here's a combination you can try:

- Step 1: Start with your feet together and your arms in first position. Plie (bend your knees), then rise up onto relevé.
- Step 2: Extend one foot to the side and raise your opposite arm to second position. Balance on relevé and hold for 3 counts.
- Step 3: Lower your foot and arm, then repeat on the other side.
- Step 4: Hold your arms in fifth position and plie, then rise up onto relevé. Balance for 5 counts.
- Step 5: Lower down to first position and finish with your arms in third position.

Remember, practice makes perfect! The more you practice these techniques, the better your balance and posture will become. Thanks for watching! context:This tutorial provides guidance on enhancing balance and posture while dancing, specifically focusing on ballet technique. Step 1: Lie on your back and extend one leg towards the ceiling. Keep your other leg bent with your foot flat on the floor. Step 2: Use your hands to grasp the back of your thigh and gently pull your leg towards your chest until you feel a stretch in the back of your leg. Step 3: Hold the stretch for 30 seconds to 1 minute, then repeat on the other leg. Stretch 2: Quad Stretch

Step 1: Stand with your feet hip-width apart and your knees slightly bent. Step 2: Lift one foot behind you and grasp onto your ankle with your hand. Step 3: Keep your knees close together and your upper body tall as you press your foot towards your buttocks to feel a stretch in the front of your leg. Step 4: Hold the stretch for 30 seconds to 1 minute, then repeat on the other leg. Stretch 3: Hip Opener

Step 1: Sit on the floor with both legs extended in front of you. Step 2: Bend your left knee and place your foot on the floor outside of your right knee. Step 3: Use your right hand to grasp onto your left knee and twist your torso to the left. Step 4: Place your left hand behind you for support and hold the stretch for 30 seconds. Repeat on the other side. Remember to never push yourself too hard and only stretch to the point of feeling a gentle stretch. content:Speaker user says: Can you summarize the main reasons for the slump in Indiana's basketball teams, including the Pacers, Hoosiers, and Butler?: IU, Butler and Pacers are in freefall at same time, for same reason.
Pacers, Hoosiers, Butler … it's hard times for a populace that puts so much of itself into its basketball teams, and is getting so little in return.
INDIANAPOLIS – Hard to be happy around here this winter, isn’t it? No sun. Too damn cold. Plus we have another reason: We’re living in a basketball state with some seriously bad basketball.
It’s not just Butler’s effort. It’s the Pacers and Hoosiers, who also suffered ugly losses Wednesday night, and whose coaches have made it clear that their teams, same as Jordan was saying of Butler, are lacking something beyond talent. Something closer to effort.
Listen to Pacers coach Nate McMillan: “It’s just low energy right now. We've kind of lost our way here and we've got to find it ... We got to get more energy in the game."
More energy? That’s code for “more effort.” Those are fighting words, or should be, if his team – if any of these teams – have any fight left.
What’s happening here? Let me take a swing at this.
When their mind’s right, the Pacers have shown this season they can win without Victor Oladipo. They were 7-4 in games without him before he suffered a torn quadriceps tendon early against the Toronto Raptors on Jan. 23, and as an example of how this team can play when its mind is right: The Pacers won that game anyway.
And the Pacers aren’t responding well. McMillan keeps saying the same thing: The Pacers need to stop focusing on who’s gone, and focus on who’s here. Clearly that’s easier to do when it's temporary, holding down the fort for a game or two as opposed to facing three months without your singular star and emotional heartbeat.
Beyond the psychological shock, losing Oladipo underscores the biggest issue with this team in an evolving NBA: Two of the Pacers’ best three players are centers, which means they rarely play together, in an era where perimeter scoring and playmaking is at a premium.
And when the only one of those three who plays the perimeter, Oladipo, goes out? Well, look: Myles Turner and Domantas Sabonis are fabulous young talents, they really are. But the Pacers need more guards. They have some young ones in Aaron Holiday and Edmond Sumner who will get more minutes. They’d better be good and ready.
And bring this team more effort, huh?
Archie Miller got tough. He called out his players after the loss to Nebraska. I was there, and it was shocking. And it didn’t work.
Will the soft touch work? Not sure it fits Miller’s style, to be honest. He’s a no-nonsense guy, a grinder, a winner as a player despite his small size, and a winner as a coach (at Dayton) by taking a roster full of overlooked recruits and turning them into something mean, something ferocious.
The Hoosiers have a better roster than Dayton ever had. But they’re not mean. Not ferocious. Archie's teams at Dayton would have eaten this IU team for lunch, and asked for another meal two hours later.
At Rutgers, where the Knights reeled off 22 consecutive points, the Hoosiers looked, frankly, soft. At Purdue they looked, frankly, scared.
A quick word about Miller: IU fans are freaking out, some of them anyway – OK, a lot of them – and wondering if Miller was the wrong guy to replace Tom Crean. And I’m telling you it’s way too soon to say that. It’s way too soon even to wonder that.
Here’s what happens when a fan base this large and passionate freaks out: It makes things so much harder on the coach, on the players, on the program. A fan base like Indiana’s, as big as it is, can be the wind in its team’s sails … or its face.
Am I blaming you, IU fans, for what has happened here? Not at all. Not any. But going forward, there is a choice to be made, and this team – as well as potential recruits – will be watching to see your decision.
Watch the players on the court, on the bench. Watch the way they interact, or in the case of Butler, the way they don’t.
The Bulldogs had no enthusiasm against Marquette, not for the game, not for each other. LaVall Jordan was blaming himself for that afterward, and up to a point, he’s right. Players can be an extension of their coach, and Jordan is cerebral. He’s a calm, quiet man, and he has a team that is too calm, too quiet. Can Jordan change the emotional makeup of his team? Can he become more like Archie, while Archie is trying to become more like LaVall?
On the Butler side, I saw pure passion one time all night Wednesday, and it was more than an hour after the game when I was leaving the Hinkle media room and heard a ball bouncing on the court. I walked to the tunnel and saw him: senior Paul Jorgensen sprinting around the court, getting up shots, working on a game that has indeed gone south. After averaging 17.2 points on 43.1-percent 3-point shooting through nine games, Jorgensen has dipped to 7.5 ppg on 34.6-percent shooting in the last 13.
Now, pay attention please: Am I blaming Paul Jorgensen for the Bulldogs’ slide from 7-2 to 12-10, and 3-6 in the Big East? Not at all. Not any. I’m bringing him up to show you what passion looks like, what caring looks like, and his was the only passion or care I saw Wednesday night. And it came an hour after the gym had emptied out.
The problems facing Butler are different from those facing the Pacers and Hoosiers, but the fixes are mostly the same: The players need to care more. The coaches need to make that happen. It’s not on somebody – it’s on everybody.
Meanwhile, in our basketball state with some really bad basketball, there’s always Purdue.

content:Speaker user says: What are the most common injuries in basketball and how are they treated? context:The user is seeking information about prevalent injuries in basketball and the methods used to manage and heal them. keywords: basketball, injuries, treatment, common tags: Sports Medicine, Injury Management, Medical Treatment

content:Speaker assistant says: 1. Ankle sprains: This is the most common injury in basketball. It occurs when the ankle twists, turns or rolls beyond its normal range of motion. Treatment includes R.I.C.E (rest, ice, compression and elevation), physical therapy, and ankle braces.

2. Knee injuries: Knee injuries commonly occur due to high-impact activities like jumping and landing, which puts a lot of strain on the knees. Common knee injuries in basketball include ACL, MCL, and meniscus tears, as well as patella tendonitis (jumper's knee). Treatment can involve physical therapy, rest, surgery, and rehabilitation.

3. Concussion: Concussions occur when there's a blow to the head or a sudden jolt that causes the brain to move back and forth in the skull. Players with a concussion should be immediately withdrawn from play and evaluated by a healthcare professional.

4. Back injuries: Basketball players may suffer from back pain or even herniated discs due to the repetitive jumping and twisting movements. Treatment includes physical therapy, rest, and surgery in severe cases.

5. Finger injuries: Finger injuries like sprains and fractures can result from injuries during ball handling, passing, or during collisions with other players. Treatment may include R.I.C.E, splinting or casting, and surgery in some cases.

Overall, prevention is key, players should maintain good physical condition, wear proper protective gear, and adhere to safety rules and proper techniques during play. context:The content addresses various injuries affecting basketball players, including ankle sprains, knee injuries, concussions, and back injuries, emphasizing the importance of prevention, appropriate treatment, and adherence to safety rules. keywords: ankle sprains, knee injuries, concussions, back injuries, finger injuries tags: Sports Injury, Physical Therapy, Player Safety
